theme: 3 terms on Swift macros: code that writes code, macros that stand alone with a hash, and macros attached with an at sign

terms.definition: A feature that generates extra Swift code for you while your app compiles.
terms.example: `#Predicate` is a Macro, so it turns this closure into a real filter.
terms.code:
import Foundation
let big = #Predicate<Int> { $0 > 3 }
let nums = [1, 5, 8]
print(try nums.filter(big))

terms.definition: A macro written with a hash sign that stands on its own and expands into code right there.
terms.example: `#line` is a Freestanding Macro, so it turns into the current line number.

terms.definition: A macro written with an at sign on a declaration that adds code to that declaration.
terms.example: `@Observable` is an Attached Macro, so it adds tracking code to the class.

quizzes.question: What do you call code generation written with an at sign on top of a type?
In this code, what kind of thing is `#function`, written with a hash sign?

video.description:
Learn to explain Swift macros: Macro, Freestanding Macro & Attached Macro, with real code, a quiz at the end and each example read twice (normal, then slow).

Today's terms
Macro - A feature that generates extra Swift code for you while your app compiles.
Freestanding Macro - A macro written with a hash sign that stands on its own and expands into code right there.
Attached Macro - A macro written with an at sign on a declaration that adds code to that declaration.

Quiz at the end - write your answers in the comments, then watch again to check.

Explain Macro, Freestanding Macro & Attached Macro in Swift by listening to a real code chat between two iOS devs.
매크로, 독립형 매크로, 부착형 매크로 표현을 영어 대화로 익혀요.

Macro - A feature that generates extra Swift code for you while your app compiles.
한국어: 매크로: 앱을 컴파일하는 동안 Swift 코드를 추가로 만들어 주는 기능

Freestanding Macro - A macro written with a hash sign that stands on its own and expands into code right there.
한국어: 독립형 매크로: # 기호로 쓰며, 혼자 서서 그 자리에서 코드로 펼쳐지는 매크로

Attached Macro - A macro written with an at sign on a declaration that adds code to that declaration.
한국어: 부착형 매크로: @ 기호로 선언 위에 붙여, 그 선언에 코드를 더해 주는 매크로

In this video, Mina and Jake sort out how a class updates the screen without extra code, what a hash sign means and how to see the generated code, in a chat-style conversation, with the Swift code on screen.

landscape.hook: Can you explain Swift macros in English?

dialogue.title: Who wrote this code?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Jake, how does SwiftUI see `volume` change? I wrote no extra code.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: `@Observable` is a Macro. It writes the tracking code when you build.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: So a Macro generates Swift code at compile time?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Yes. This one is an Attached Macro, because it sits on `Settings`.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: What about `#line` in `log`? It has a hash sign.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That's a Freestanding Macro. It becomes the line number.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Wait, I thought `#line` was just a special keyword.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: It used to be. Now Swift declares it as a Freestanding Macro.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Can I see what an Attached Macro adds?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Sure. In Xcode, right-click `@Observable` and expand it.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Got it. Freestanding Macro with a hash, Attached Macro with an at sign.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Who wrote all this hidden code?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: A Macro did, at compile time.
